title: Former SBI Manager Quits Over Burnout, Opens Yoga Studio in UP
excerpt: A woman working as an assistant manager at the State Bank of India has quit her job, citing constant stress and mental exhaustion, and opened her own yoga studio in Uttar Pradesh — a story picked up by five national outlets that has become one of the week's most-shared conversations about work and wellbeing.
body:
• A woman working as an assistant manager at the State Bank of India has quit her job, citing constant stress and mental exhaustion.
  • She has opened her own yoga studio in Uttar Pradesh, turning to the discipline she credits with restoring her sense of balance.
  • The story has been covered by the Hindustan Times, Moneycontrol, NDTV, News18 and The Times of India, becoming one of the week's most-shared trending stories in India.
  • It feeds a growing public conversation about burnout, mental health and the true cost of secure, high-pressure jobs in India's public-sector banking.

Walking away from a "secure" job

In India, a job at the State Bank of India is considered the gold standard of professional security — a government-backed position with a pension, status and a clear ladder. A woman who had climbed to assistant manager has now walked away from it, telling interviewers that constant stress and mental exhaustion made the position unsustainable. In its place, she has opened her own yoga studio in Uttar Pradesh.

The story broke across five national outlets — the Hindustan Times, Moneycontrol, NDTV, News18 and The Times of India — and quickly became one of the most-shared trending stories of the week. According to Moneycontrol's report, she described the pressure of the job as relentless, and said the decision to leave was about reclaiming her health rather than chasing a bigger paycheck.

Why this one resonated

Quitting a government bank job is a culturally loaded act in India, where "sarkari naukri" remains the aspiration of millions of families. Stories like this one keep going viral because they give public voice to a private calculation many are making: a year ago, a 29-year-old Delhi woman who worked as a Scale-I officer at Punjab National Bank quit after being posted to Meerut, writing on Instagram that she was choosing "mental peace" over financial stability — that post crossed 5 million views, according to LatestLY.

The pattern is hard to miss. SBI is the country's largest lender, with some 2.36 lakh employees, and the pressure of targets, transfers and customer volumes in public-sector banking is well documented. In a telling sign of the times, SBI itself announced last year that it would host virtual yoga sessions twice a week for its workforce and train all employees under a financial-planning certification framework — an institutional acknowledgment that wellbeing has become a retention issue, according to Devdiscourse.

The burnout conversation in India

Mental health at work has moved from whispered concern to open debate in India over the past few years. The World Health Organization defines burnout as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed — characterized by exhaustion, mental distance from the job, and reduced professional efficacy. What makes stories like the former SBI manager's land is their specificity: this isn't abstract advice about work-life balance, it's a person trading a pension for a yoga mat and saying so publicly.

Her choice of a second act is equally Indian. Yoga's global commercial boom — studios, teacher-training programs, corporate wellness contracts — has created a genuine alternative economy for people exiting high-stress careers. Whether a single studio in Uttar Pradesh can match a bank manager's salary is an open question; she appears to have decided the comparison itself was the problem.

Diaspora angle

The trade-off she named — security versus sanity — is one the Indian diaspora knows intimately. Banking, consulting and tech jobs in the US, UK and Canada carry the same grind, and the "quit the job, find yourself" genre performs just as well among NRIs. Her story offers diaspora readers a familiar mirror, with one difference: the fallback she chose, yoga, is an Indian export the world already takes seriously.

What's next

The studio is open; the audience is watching. Viral stories like this one tend to bring both students and scrutiny — whether the business sustains her will be the real test of the decision. Either way, the conversation it triggered shows no sign of fading: each public resignation reframes the question for the millions still in their seats, from what a good job pays to what it costs.
nri_angle: Indian professionals abroad — where banking, consulting and tech jobs carry the same grind — are having the same conversation about burnout and exit plans; this story lands because the trade-off between a secure job and mental health translates across borders.
author: Diaspora Desk
